parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Bike workshop note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Marta,

I finally took my commuter bike to the neighbourhood repair hub yesterday because the back brake was rubbing badly. Although I worried it would cost a fortune, the mechanic only [1] a small fee for a new cable. While I waited, he showed me how to [2] an eye on tyre pressure so I do not get another flat tyre. Next Saturday the hub is running a free roadside repair evening, [3] sounds really useful for daily riders. They also [4] a pump and spare inner tubes for anyone who forgets theirs. Let me know if you feel like coming [5] with me!

Best,
Ethan

questions.explanation: 'Charged a small fee' is used when a shop or mechanic asks a customer to pay an amount; 'paid' and 'earned' do not fit the mechanic's role.
'Keep an eye on' is a fixed collocation meaning to watch or check something regularly.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause after a comma, referring back to the free roadside repair evening.
'Offer a pump and spare inner tubes' matches the plural subject 'they' and means making equipment available; 'lends' is singular and 'present' does not fit.
'Come along with me' is the phrasal verb meaning to accompany someone to an event.

parts.title: Text cohesion: Fixing a flat tyre
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Halfway through my morning ride to the office, I heard a sharp hiss and felt the back wheel bump heavily over the tarmac. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: After pulling out a tiny piece of broken glass, I fitted a fresh inner tube inside the tyre.
I pushed my bike onto the pavement, turned it upside down, and released the rear wheel.
Finally, I clicked the wheel back into the frame and arrived at work only ten minutes late.
Then I used two plastic levers to lift one edge of the rubber tyre off the metal rim.
Once the new tube sat neatly in place, I pumped it up firmly with my pocket mini-pump.

gaps.explanation: After hearing the hiss and feeling the bump, the rider first moves off the road onto the pavement and removes the rear wheel.
'Then I used two plastic levers' follows removing the wheel and describes lifting the tyre off the rim to reach the inner tube.
Once the tyre is lifted off the rim, the rider finds the broken glass and fits a fresh inner tube inside.
'Once the new tube sat neatly in place' refers directly to the fresh inner tube in the previous sentence and introduces pumping it up.
'Finally, I clicked the wheel back into the frame' closes the repair sequence and explains arriving at work.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Cycling in the city
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about cycling in the city. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Lottie
texts.text: I started cycling to work two years ago mainly to avoid crowded buses, and now I cannot imagine going back. Even so, painted white lines on busy roads do not make me feel safe when delivery vans park right across them. What really encourages ordinary people to ride is a separate lane with a raised kerb between bikes and cars. I also wish offices offered warm showers, though a basic covered rack outside the front door already helps a lot.

texts.title: Jamal
texts.text: People often assume you need an expensive lightweight bicycle for city commuting, yet my heavy second-hand steel bike has survived five rainy winters without a single serious fault. In my view, learning how to oil your own chain and adjust brake pads saves far more money than buying fancy gear. When a minor squeak appears, I fix it on Sunday afternoon with a ten-euro toolkit rather than paying a shop every month.

texts.title: Oscar
texts.text: Using our city's shared electric bikes has completely changed my evenings. Because the hills around my flat are steep, I used to arrive at friends' houses soaked in sweat on a normal bike. Now I can pick up an e-bike outside the station, ride home effortlessly in work clothes, and drop it at the dock near my street. The only downside is that the docks near the park sometimes have no bikes left after six o'clock.

texts.title: Nina
texts.text: As a keen commuter, I love how quickly a bike gets me through morning traffic, and I never waste time hunting for a parking space. However, I think cyclists themselves also need to follow traffic lights and slow down near pedestrians. Whenever a rider speeds through a red light, it makes drivers angry at all of us. Clearer road markings help, of course, but polite behaviour from everyone on the street matters just as much.

questions.explanation: Lottie says painted white lines are not enough and that a separate lane with a raised kerb between bikes and cars encourages people to ride safely.
Jamal rides a cheap second-hand steel bike and says learning to oil the chain and adjust brake pads saves more money than buying fancy gear.
Oscar explains that shared electric bikes let him ride up steep hills to friends' houses in work clothes instead of arriving soaked in sweat.
Nina says cyclists need to follow traffic lights and slow down near pedestrians, noting that polite behaviour from everyone matters.
Oscar points out that the shared e-bike docks near the park sometimes have no bikes left after six o'clock.
Lottie mentions that while warm office showers would be nice, a basic covered rack outside the front door already helps a lot.
Nina loves how quickly a bike gets her through morning traffic and says she never wastes time hunting for a parking space.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: How the city bicycle evolved
parts.instructions: Read the article about city cycling and bicycle design. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: When the first modern-looking bicycles appeared on European streets in the late nineteenth century, they did far more than entertain weekend sports clubs. Fitted with two equal-sized wheels, a chain drive, and air-filled rubber tyres, the new 'safety bicycle' was stable enough for ordinary commuters of all ages. Factory workers could suddenly live several kilometres from noisy workshops, while women gained affordable independence to travel across town without waiting for a carriage or a chaperone.

For several decades after the Second World War, however, city planners across many countries focused almost entirely on private cars. Wide streets were rebuilt to move motor traffic faster, tram lines were torn up, and narrow cycling paths disappeared under rows of parked vehicles. Cycling in town came to be seen either as a child's toy or as a risky habit for brave athletes, causing everyday commuter numbers to drop sharply in major capitals.

A turning point arrived in the 1970s, when fuel shortages and rising road accidents pushed citizens in several European cities to demand safer streets. Local residents organised weekend street protests, painting temporary cycle lanes and calling for car-free squares around schools. City councils gradually listened, creating connected networks of separated bike paths and safer junctions. Where protected routes were built, families and older riders quickly returned to the saddle.

Today's urban bicycles look very different from the heavy single-gear machines of a century ago. Aluminium frames keep weight low when carrying a bike up apartment stairs, while internal hub gears stay clean inside a sealed case even in winter rain. Automatic dynamo lights powered by the front wheel mean commuters never have to worry about flat batteries on dark evenings, and puncture-resistant tyres reduce roadside delays on broken glass.

Keeping a city bike reliable does not require a garage full of specialist tools. Most mechanics agree that three simple weekly habits prevent the majority of expensive repairs. Pumping tyres to the recommended pressure stops pinch flats and makes pedalling feel noticeably lighter. Wiping grit off the chain with an old cloth and adding a drop of oil keeps gears shifting smoothly, while squeezing brake levers before setting off catches worn pads early.

Alongside private bikes, public bike-sharing schemes and electric cargo bikes are reshaping how goods and people move through dense neighbourhoods. Commuters can unlock a shared bike near a train station for the final two kilometres to work without worrying about theft overnight. Meanwhile, small bakeries, florists, and courier firms are replacing noisy delivery vans with electric cargo bikes that carry heavy boxes past traffic jams right to the customer's door.

To keep up with this growing demand, many neighbourhoods now host community bike kitchens where volunteers teach riders to repair their own machines. Instead of dropping a broken bike at a busy shop and paying high labour costs, members borrow professional stands, spanners, and wheel-truing tools for a small donation. Learning to replace a snapped cable or straighten a rubbing brake builds practical confidence and keeps older bicycles out of landfill.

headings: Everyday habits that prevent costly breakdowns
Why post-war cities pushed bicycles off the road
Community workshops teach riders self-repair skills
Shared fleets and cargo bikes transform urban trips
How professional road races changed helmet rules
Modern features designed for all-weather commuting
Public campaigns bring protected lanes back to towns
An early design that offered everyday freedom

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes how the nineteenth-century safety bicycle gave factory workers and women affordable, independent everyday travel.
Paragraph 2 explains how post-war planners prioritized cars, removed cycle paths, and caused everyday cycling numbers to fall.
Paragraph 3 focuses on 1970s citizen protests and campaigns that convinced councils to build connected networks of protected bike lanes.
Paragraph 4 details modern commuter features such as aluminium frames, sealed gears, dynamo lights, and puncture-resistant tyres.
Paragraph 5 outlines three simple weekly maintenance habits—checking tyre pressure, cleaning the chain, and testing brakes—that avoid costly repairs.
Paragraph 6 explains how bike-sharing schemes and electric cargo bikes are changing commuting and local deliveries in dense cities.
Paragraph 7 describes community bike kitchens where volunteers help riders borrow tools and learn to fix their own bicycles.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a transport planner about a new city bike lane (questions 1-2), then a bike mechanic about running a mobile repair van (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Oscar, a transport planner, talking about a new protected cycle lane along Market Street.

turns.speaker: oscar
turns.text: When our council announced plans to remove one lane of car parking on Market Street to build a protected cycle path, shopkeepers feared they would lose half their regular customers overnight. I understood why they felt nervous, because delivery lorries also needed space to unload boxes every morning. Instead of forcing the design through quickly, our team spent three weeks standing outside cafés and bakeries, counting how visitors actually arrived. It turned out that nearly seventy percent of local shoppers walked or arrived by bus, and very few parked right outside the shops. We adjusted the layout to leave two clear loading bays for lorries while giving cyclists a safe kerb-separated track. Six months after opening, we expected weekend leisure riders to use it most. What genuinely surprised everyone was that morning commuter numbers doubled, and several cafés added extra pavement tables because the street felt noticeably quieter and cleaner.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Cora, a bicycle mechanic, talking about starting her mobile bike repair van.

turns.speaker: cora
turns.text: Three years ago I worked in a busy city-centre bike shop, and I kept noticing the same problem: customers with flat tyres or broken gears often waited four days just to drop their bikes off, because they couldn't carry a heavy bike onto a bus during work hours. That's what pushed me to fit a workbench, wheel stand, and tool drawers inside a small electric van and drive directly to office car parks and apartment blocks. People assume the trickiest part of working from a van is dealing with rain or cold winter winds. Honestly, a pop-up canopy solves bad weather easily. The real challenge has been predicting which spare parts to pack each morning, since running out of one specific brake pad means wasting an hour driving back to the storeroom. If another mechanic asked me how to start a mobile service, I'd tell them not to advertise across the whole city at first. Focus on two or three busy neighbourhoods so you spend your day fixing bikes rather than sitting in traffic.

questions.prompt: Why did Oscar's team count visitors outside cafés and bakeries before building the lane?

To find the cheapest place for new bus stops
To persuade delivery drivers to work at night
questions.explanation: Oscar says shopkeepers feared losing driving customers, so his team counted how visitors actually arrived and found most walked or took the bus.

questions.prompt: What surprised Oscar most six months after the Market Street lane opened?
options: Weekend leisure riders avoided the busy centre

questions.explanation: Oscar expected weekend leisure riders to use it most, so he was genuinely surprised that morning commuter numbers doubled.

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you had to solve a practical transport or travel problem. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Describe a time when a journey did not go as planned or something broke on the way.
2. How did you solve the problem, and how did you feel afterwards?
3. Why do you think more cities are encouraging people to cycle instead of driving?
